content:
The [Compound Growth Calculator](/compound-growth-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. How an amount grows at a steady rate — the power of compounding over time. Enter your starting amount, annual growth rate, years and compounding and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Compound growth is what happens when growth earns growth: each year's increase is added to the balance, so the next year's growth is calculated on a larger amount. The effect is small at first and dramatic later — the last few years of a long period add far more than the first few. This calculator shows the future value of a single amount growing at a steady rate, with no extra contributions. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Compound Growth Calculator

Start by entering your starting amount, then entering your annual growth rate (%), entering your years and finally choosing your compounding from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the starting amount — the sum you begin with.
2. Enter the annual growth rate as a percentage.
3. Set the number of years and how often growth compounds.
4. Compare the future value with the starting amount to see the growth.

## Formula

Future value = P × (1 + r/n)^(n×t), where P is the starting amount, r the annual growth rate, n the compounding periods per year and t the years.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Compound Growth Calculator](/compound-growth-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. $10,000 growing at 8% a year becomes $21,589.25 after 10 years — a gain of $11,589.25, or 2.16 times your money. At the same rate for 20 years it reaches $46,609.57. Try the same figures in the [Compound Growth Calculator](/compound-growth-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Starting amount: 10000, Annual growth rate: 8 %, Years: 10, Compounding: Yearly), the [Compound Growth Calculator](/compound-growth-calculator) returns Future value: 21,589.25, Growth: 11,589.25, Times your money: 2.16×, Growth per year (average): 1,158.92. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## The power of compounding

Compounding is exponential, not linear. At 8% a year, $10,000 doubles in about 9 years (the Rule of 72: 72 ÷ 8 ≈ 9). The first doubling takes 9 years; the second takes another 9 — but it adds twice as much money. That is why the same rate produces such different results over 10, 20 and 30 years, and why starting early matters far more than starting big.

## Nominal vs real growth

The rate you enter is nominal — it ignores inflation. If prices rise 3% a year, an 8% nominal return is only about 5% in real terms. For a figure in today's purchasing power, enter the real rate (nominal minus inflation). For the amount you will actually see in your account in future, enter the nominal rate.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- The Rule of 72: divide 72 by the rate to estimate the years needed to double.
- Small rate differences compound enormously over decades — 7% vs 8% over 30 years is a 35% difference in the final value.
- Growth is assumed steady here; real investments vary year to year.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the difference between simple and compound growth?

Simple growth adds the same amount every year (rate × starting amount). Compound growth adds a growing amount, because each year's growth is calculated on the new, larger balance. Try it with your own numbers in the [Compound Growth Calculator](/compound-growth-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How long will it take to double my money?

Roughly 72 divided by the annual rate: at 8%, about 9 years; at 6%, about 12 years. That is the Rule of 72. Try it with your own numbers in the [Compound Growth Calculator](/compound-growth-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does compounding frequency matter much?

A little. Monthly compounding earns slightly more than yearly at the same rate, but the difference is small compared with the rate itself and the time period. Try it with your own numbers in the [Compound Growth Calculator](/compound-growth-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Compound Growth Calculator use?

Future value = P × (1 + r/n)^(n×t), where P is the starting amount, r the annual growth rate, n the compounding periods per year and t the years. You can see it in action in the [Compound Growth Calculator](/compound-growth-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
